# The Peculiar Joy of Getting Lost

There's something oddly liberating about being completely, utterly lost. Not the panic-stricken kind where your phone dies and you're genuinely worried about missing an important meeting, but the genuine, wandering-through-an-unfamiliar-city-with-nowhere-to-be kind of lost. The kind that turns into adventure.

I've been thinking about this a lot lately, particularly after realizing how rare this feeling has become in modern life. We have GPS satellites following our every movement, Google Maps knowing every street corner, our phones vibrating with reminders about where we're supposed to be next. We've engineered uncertainty almost entirely out of our existence, and in doing so, we've removed something that humans actually need—the surprise, the discovery, the chance encounter.

When I was a kid, getting lost was practically inevitable. My friends and I would set out on our bikes with vague destinations in mind, and inevitably we'd end up in parts of town we'd never seen before. We'd discover weird little gardens tucked behind residential streets, find tiny cafes that seemed to exist in their own pocket dimension, stumble upon used bookstores run by ancient men who knew every volume in their inventory by heart. There was no way to quickly verify if we were heading in the right direction. We just had to follow our intuition, ask strangers, or keep riding until something felt recognizable.

Those discoveries seemed magical because they were genuinely accidental. We could never quite retrace our steps to those places. They existed in memory rather than in GPS coordinates, which made them feel more real somehow, more truly ours.

Now I'm an adult, and I've been thinking about how this relates to bigger things—like how we've systematized most of human experience. We have optimal routes to everything, algorithms that predict what we'll want before we want it, career paths that are well-trodden and mapped out. We're encouraged to be efficient, to minimize wasted time, to know what we're doing and where we're going.

But there's a cost to all this optimization. Somewhere in the process of removing friction from our lives, we've also removed the possibility of genuine surprise. And surprise—that moment when you turn a corner and see something you weren't expecting—is what makes you feel alive.

I wonder if this is why some of the most interesting conversations I have happen with strangers in unexpected places. There's something about the randomness of it that opens people up. You meet someone at a bus stop, and because you'll probably never see them again, they tell you something true. You're not performing for anyone. There's no social media audience. It's just two people, briefly connected by geography and circumstance rather than algorithm.

The internet promised to connect us to everyone, but in practice, it's mostly connected us to people exactly like ourselves. The algorithm learns what you like and shows you more of it. You follow people whose opinions you already agree with. You end up in these bubbles that feel diverse until you realize everyone around you has read the same articles and shares the same references.

Getting lost—real, old-fashioned, analog getting lost—is the opposite of this. It forces you to encounter the world as it actually is, not as a curated collection designed for your consumption. It makes you vulnerable. You have to ask for help, which means talking to actual humans. You have to trust your instincts, which might be wrong. You might end up somewhere weird or uncomfortable, but you might also find something wonderful.

I've started deliberately getting lost in cities I visit. I'll leave my phone at the hotel or ignore it completely and just walk, turning whenever something catches my eye. It sounds like a small thing, but it feels radical. My friends think I'm insane. "Why wouldn't you just use Google Maps?" they ask, genuinely confused.

The answer is harder to articulate than it should be. Because I want to remember this city as something I discovered, not something I navigated. Because the inefficient path is usually more interesting. Because the detour is where the story is.

There's also something about the feeling of being lost that makes you more present. You can't walk on autopilot when you're not sure where you are. You notice things—the architecture of buildings, the smell of a restaurant, the way light hits a street corner at a particular time of day. You're more alert, more alive, because your brain isn't already three steps ahead of where you're going.

I think about teenagers today, and I wonder what they're missing. They have maps but not mysteries. They have connection but not coincidence. Everything is arranged for them, optimized for their preferences, predicted before they even know they want it. Where do they learn to trust their instincts? Where do they experience genuine surprise? How do they develop the kind of confidence that comes from figuring things out on your own?

Maybe this is why people seem so anxious now. We've removed all the small risks from life—the possibility of getting lost, of being late, of showing up somewhere and finding it closed or different than expected—but we haven't made ourselves feel safer. Instead, we've just become more fragile. We've outsourced our navigation to machines, and in doing so, we've forgotten how to navigate ourselves.

So I'm going to keep getting lost. I'm going to turn down streets without knowing where they lead. I'm going to talk to strangers and take detours and show up late because I got distracted by something interesting. I'm going to make mistakes in a world that doesn't require perfection.

Because there's something about confusion and discovery that's essential to being human. Not the anxiety kind of confusion, but the good kind—the kind that precedes learning something, that comes right before you understand something new about the world or yourself.

The future doesn't have to be a place we navigate toward. Sometimes it's better to wander in its direction and see what we find.
